items.en: “Its contract with insurers provides that ‘CCC may use data to train AI Services,'” the complaint states. “Its contract with repair facilities reserves to CCC the use of the facility’s data for CCC’s own ‘product improvement, and research and development,’ a use that ‘may continue after the expiration or termination of this agreement.’ CCC tells consumers none of this. No page of the estimate describes CCC’s retention, aggregation, or commercial use of the personal information, or gives the consumer any way to opt out of it, see it, or delete it.”

According to the suit, the Repair Facility License Agreement “authorizes CCC to provide the repair ‘content’ to insurers whose direct repair programs the shop participates in, or with whom the shop configures CCC ONE UpdatePlus to share information, and separately authorizes CCC to provide the Content to CCC’s vendor, Flash of Genius, Inc. (d/b/a UpdatePromise) (“Flash”), granting the identified insurers, CCC, and that vendor ‘perpetual, royalty-free licenses to use the content.'”
The agreement also “forbids the repair facility itself to ‘compile estimate data for the purpose of creating a database,’ a use that CCC reserves to itself…”

The Appraiser License Agreement also forbids the appraiser to “‘compile estimate data for the purpose of creating a database'” and “‘aggregate or co-mingle data in the programs and/or services or provide reports or analysis based on data in the programs and/or services to anyone.'”

It notes as well that a section of the Insurer MSA, titled “License by Customer to CCC,” “contemplates the development or testing of artificial intelligence tools or models on Customer Data that has not been de-identified, subject only to the customer’s prior written approval, which the provision states CCC may accept by e-mail from a vice-president-level or higher employee of the customer.”
The plaintiffs contend that consumers aren’t parties or signatories to the aforementioned agreements despite CCC’s collection, movement, and licensing of their personal information.

“The Repair Facility License Agreement runs between CCC and a collision repair facility, the Appraiser License Agreement runs between CCC and an independent appraiser, and the Insurer MSA and DPA run between CCC and an insurer,” the suit states.

“The only authorization CCC obtains to take and use consumers’ personal information under these agreements is the business’s own promise: under the Repair Facility License Agreement, customer ‘represents and warrants that it has full right and authority to provide the authorization and licenses contained herein,’ and indemnifies CCC ‘for failure to obtain the requisite authorizations;’ and under the Appraiser License Agreement, customer ‘represents and warrants that it has the right to provide the data to CCC.'”

The suit also states that CCC has patented training AI models on identifiable consumer data and harvesting vehicle event data recorder information, including U.S. Patent No. 10,922,726; U.S. Patent No. 11,727,551; and U.S. Patent No. 9,500,545.

“Taken together, these patents describe CCC’s designs for systems that ingest, store, retrain on, and reuse identifiable consumer and vehicle data of the kinds that populate CCC ONE, including names, home addresses, VINs, license plates, policy and claim identifiers, and event-data-recorder data,” the suit states. “On information and belief, CCC has implemented these designs in the CCC ONE platform and in the artificial-intelligence products and analytics it licenses to insurers and other customers.”

The proposed nationwide class includes more than 15 million U.S. vehicle owners or customers named on repair estimates that a U.S. collision repair facility prepared on CCC ONE in the four years before the complaint was filed. It also proposes a nationwide intrusion subclass and a California subclass.

Relief sought includes nominal and punitive damages, restitution and disgorgement of the value CCC obtained from consumers’ information, barring CCC from using consumer information for AI training or other purposes beyond the estimate without consent, and requiring CCC to delete consumer PII.

An injunction on behalf of the California subclass would require CCC to inform California consumers before or when their personal information is entered into CCC ONE at a collision repair facility of its identity, the categories of PII it collects, and the purposes of use for the PII. It would also require CCC to obtain consumer consent before using PII for any purpose beyond preparing or transmitting vehicle estimates or valuations.
CCC hadn’t filed a response to the suit in court as of Monday afternoon.

“Artificial intelligence is reshaping the economy, and the question of what these systems are built on has never mattered more,” said Maro Burunsuzyan, attorney for the plaintiffs and founder of the Law Offices of Maro Burunsuzyan, in a press release.

“The complaint alleges that, in CCC’s case, part of the answer is the personal information of ordinary people who simply needed a car repaired. Those drivers were never told, never asked, and never paid. This case is about restoring a basic principle: a company that wants to profit from your information should have to ask you first.”

Off-Highway Brake & Friction Excellence is All-Italian

SK Wellman, a company specializing in the production of brake and frictions components for off-highway, has a lively DNA. A historical reality in Orzinuovi (Bs), where the plant is still located, over the years it has undergone transformations and changes that have contributed to making it what it is today: an evolved company, able to grow in loyalty to the local Italian territory and to innovate its sector with creativity and flexibility worldwide. Today, as part of the CentroMotion Group and its Carlisle Brake & Friction division, SK Wellman is a leader in its segment, recognized and chosen by major brands in earthmoving, agricultural and construction machinery. Engineer Alessandro Gamba, Global Director of Friction Engineering, tells us about the ongoing growth.

"S.K. Wellman S.R.L. has 340 employees and a turnover of 127 million by 2023," Gamba begins. In the last five years, a strong push has come from the market but above all from the characteristics of SK, such as creativity, innovation, flexibility, which, in the final analysis, are the result of the greatest wealth of this company: people". They are the ones who make the Brescia-based company an authentic and tenacious company, to the point of being able to export not only their products successfully, but also their skills and design skills to the other plants of the Carlisle Brake & Friction division. The year 2023, which has just ended, confirms a positive performance in turnover for sales revenues alone, recording a slight decrease of -5% compared to the previous exceptional 2022 financial year; A year, the latter, probably unrepeatable for many realities of the Brescia and non-Brescia economy. In fact, 2023 was undoubtedly the year of change that helped people develop a greater ability to manage uncertainty, accepting and dealing with unexpected situations with more resilience.

"At the base of success there is a matrix organization developed thanks to group governance - explains the engineer -: a verticality driven on all functions and skills, able to define and guide processes on a global scale and generate best practices. And that's not all," adds Gamba, "we are one of the companies with the lowest level of turnover, and this allows us to transfer the experience of those who have been with us for a long time to young people, on whom we particularly focus. Added to this is a company population of 15 different nationalities, whose strong collaboration creates a truly serene working climate," says the HR Manager. It is no coincidence that the direction of growth is particularly social responsibility.

"Among the main projects of SK Wellman and Carlisle - he observes - stands out Enactus, an international non-profit organization that, thanks to its activity, involves university students in the creation of sustainable entrepreneurial projects, helping to bridge the gap between university and business; and then Treedom, which involves the company's commitment to planting 1,600 trees in three years, involving its stakeholders in the project". Two more rare gems for the metalworking industry? A level of accidents at work that borders on zero, and the centrality of talent development. Towards excellence and beyond.
Source: Il Corriere della Sera – edizione Lombardia

“For too long, safety in the automotive industry has not worked equally well for everyone,” says Åsa Haglund, Volvo head of Cars Safety Centre, in the release. “At Volvo Cars, we’ve taken a different approach. By studying real-world crashes and designing with the needs of women, men and children of all body types in mind, we’ve worked for decades to provide a high level of protection regardless of who you are or where you sit in the car. Our latest research confirms that equal protection is not just an ambition, but something we have been able to achieve in Volvo cars for many years.”

At the SEMA Show next month, active safety engineers from General Motors and Ford will provide a look behind the engineering decisions that influence vehicle safety before, during, and after a collision.

They’ll speak during the second session of the Society of Collision Repair Specialists’ (SCRS) 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit, titled “Engineering the Safety Benefit: From Requirements to Real-World Performance,” Thursday, Nov. 5, from 2–3 p.m.

It will follow an earlier session featuring National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Deputy Administrator Lee White from 12:30–1:30 p.m. White will examine vehicle safety priorities and the agency’s role in advancing safety on U.S. roadways.
To register for all three OEM Summit sessions, visit here.
An SCRS RDE Full Series Pass provides access to Tuesday and Wednesday RDE sessions, the IDEAS Collide Showcase, Thursday’s OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit, and the SCRS Afterparty.

“This second session will move from those broader safety objectives into the vehicle itself, examining how automakers translate requirements and safety goals into technologies designed to produce measurable real-world benefits,” an SCRS press release states. “The afternoon will then progress to the collision repair environment, exploring how those engineered capabilities are preserved and restored after a vehicle has been damaged.”

The second session will bring together engineers who are responsible for developing, evaluating, and measuring advanced vehicle safety systems. Attendees will learn about the engineering decisions that influence vehicle safety.

Panelists include Michael Carpenter, General Motors Active Safety and Global Vehicle Performance owner; Jameson Collins, General Motors Active Safety and staff product manager; and Jeremy Nelson, Ford Motor Co. ADAS application systems engineer.

Carpenter works within GM Global Product Safety, Systems, and Certification on ADAS technology and performance strategies, new technology development, implementation of regulatory and consumer metric requirements, ADAS field effectiveness and safety benefits, and industry collaboration on standards and test-method development.

Collins leads product strategy, roadmap development, and delivery for GM’s Active Safety features, translating customer needs, competitive insights, and regulatory requirements into technologies intended to improve safety and the driving experience.

Nelson focuses on the development, release, integration, and servicing of advanced driver assistance system domain controllers. He supports vehicle production and development milestones while troubleshooting ADAS components and working across engineering, quality, and product development teams to ensure systems perform safely and as intended.

The discussion will be moderated by Jake Rodenroth, automotive industry executive, and will move beyond what ADAS features do to examine why they exist, how their intended performance is established, and how their effectiveness is evaluated. This will include what it means when a safety system is absent, disabled, damaged, or operating outside its intended parameters.

The release states: “That progression leads directly to a fundamental question for collision repair professionals: If a vehicle entered a collision with a measurable safety capability, how can the repairer know that capability has been restored?”

The panel will also explore ADAS feature development, real-world effectiveness, crash avoidance and mitigation, implications of inoperable systems, verification of safety performance, and the potential for system degradation.
The 2026 OEM Collision Repair Technology Summit is part of SCRS’ Repairer Driven Education (RDE) program at the SEMA Show.

“The Summit brings collision repair professionals together with automakers, engineers, regulators, and other subject-matter experts to examine emerging technologies and their implications for safe and complete vehicle repair,” the release states.

During the first session, White will present on the agency’s current vehicle and roadway safety priorities, emerging transportation technologies, data-driven research, and the federal government’s work with the industry to reduce fatalities and serious injuries, an SCRS release states.

Following White’s presentation, he will sit down with Aaron Schulenburg, SCRS executive director, for a one-on-one conversation exploring the intersection between federal safety objectives, automotive innovation, and the collision repair industry’s role in preserving vehicle safety throughout its service life.
NHTSA sits at the center of many discussions that impact the collision repair industry.

During a July Collision Industry Conference meeting, Schulenburg discussed NHTSA’s investigation into counterfeit airbags with Teena Bohi, an Automotive Anti-Counterfeiting Council (A2C2) Board member.

In April, NHTSA announced a ban on one type of counterfeit airbag part. Before the ban, it also issued an “urgent” industry alert specifically asking the auto repair industry to look for dangerous airbag inflators.
Repair procedures are impacted by NHTSA-mandated vehicle safety technology. This includes mandated backup cameras in all new vehicles under 10,000 pounds as of May 2018.
NHTSA also has a final rule that mandates automatic emergency braking (AEB) in pedestrian vehicles by September 2029.
However, NHTSA also announced it paused the rule to give the Trump administration time to review it following pushback and a lawsuit filed by the Alliance of Automotive Innovation (Auto Innovators).
Additional information about SCRS and RDE can be found at www.scrs.come/rde
For more information about SCRS or to join as a member, visit www.scrs.com, call 877-841-0660, or email [email protected]
Fix Auto USA has announced the opening of Fix Auto South Salt Lake, located at 3218 S W Temple Street in South Salt Lake, Utah.

Owned and operated by Efrain Perez, Fix Auto South Salt Lake is Perez’s third Fix Auto USA location and further expands his commitment to delivering high-quality collision repair services while maintaining a strong focus on family values, customer care and community involvement.

The approximately 14,000-square-foot facility is staffed by a team of five professionals and is equipped to provide full-service collision repair with room to support future growth. Services include body and structural repairs, estimating, refinishing and paint matching, parts replacement, vehicle diagnostics, glass replacement and post-repair calibrations. The shop works with all insurance carriers and assists customers throughout the claims and repair process to ensure a seamless repair experience.
For Perez, the collision repair industry is more than a profession. It’s a lifelong passion rooted in family and tradition.

“I grew up in my father’s body shop in Colombia, surrounded by the sounds of tools, welding sparks, bodywork and fresh paint,” said Perez. “Although my father hoped I would choose an easier career, I was drawn to the industry and learned by watching him and helping wherever I could. He taught me honesty, responsibility, hard work and the importance of being proud of anything that carries your name. Today, owning three body shops is something I am incredibly grateful for, and the values my father instilled in me continue to guide how we serve our customers and community every day.”
Perez added that the business has become a true family endeavor.

“What makes this journey especially meaningful is that Fix Auto USA has become a family business in every sense. My wife, Rebeca, serves as co-owner and general manager, and my brother, my son, several close friends and even my father are actively involved in the business. Seeing everything come full circle, from growing up in my father’s shop in Colombia to building this business together as a family, is incredibly special.”
As the South Salt Lake location grows, the team looks forward to supporting local families, schools, youth programs and community events while building lasting relationships throughout the region.

“We joined Fix Auto because its values align with our commitment to quality, integrity and customer service,” said Perez. “The franchise provides strong operational support, industry resources, national brand recognition and access to a trusted network, while still allowing us to remain locally owned and actively involved in our community.”

“Efrain’s story is a powerful example of entrepreneurship, perseverance and dedication to the collision repair industry,” said Damien Reyna, COO, Driven Brand Collision Group. “From learning the trade in his father’s shop in Colombia to building a successful multi-location business in the U.S., Efrain has remained committed to quality repairs, exceptional customer service and investing in the communities he serves. We are proud to celebrate the opening of Fix Auto South Salt Lake and welcome this location to the growing Fix Auto USA network.”
For more information on Fix Auto USA, visit FixAutoUSA.com.
ADAS Assist has announced the launch of its calibration verification and business management platform for collision repair shops and ADAS calibration providers.
Built by collision and calibration professionals, ADAS Assist is designed to close the accuracy gap when required calibrations are missed after a repair.

Modern vehicles rely on cameras, radars and sensors often located where collisions occur. Determining which calibrations a repair requires means matching each line of a collision estimate to the correct OEM procedure. A single miss can lead to a safety failure, liability claim or comeback. The ADAS Assist team said they experienced that risk firsthand and relied on a third-party scrubbing tool with real-world accuracy around 70%. After finding similar shortcomings in other tools, they decided to build their own.

“In ADAS calibration, accuracy is not a ‘nice to have’, it’s a ‘got to have,’” said James Rodis of ADAS Assist. “A 30% margin for error was not something we could keep living with. We are not programmers. We are collision professionals who have run shops, managed technicians and answered for a missed calibration. We built ADAS Assist because we needed it ourselves first.”

- ADAS Verification System (AVS): A quoting and scrubbing engine that reads a body shop estimate and identifies the required calibrations and related operations. AVS releases nothing until it clears well over 90% confidence, ties each operation to the estimate line that triggered it, and links directly to the governing OEM procedure so technicians and estimators can see exactly what is required and why.

- Customer Management System (CMS): Built to run the calibration operation for body shops and calibration centers from one place, including custom pricing, technician management, a daily technician calendar, job scheduling and invoicing.

Shops submit requests by uploading an estimate and answering questions about the vehicle’s damage. They receive a documented quote for the vehicle’s VIN, along with direct access to the supporting OEM documentation.

“AVS and CMS were built to work together, not as two separate tools stapled to one login,” Rodis said. “That is how the work actually flows in a real shop, and it is what sets ADAS Assist apart from tools designed by people who have never stood in a bay.
“Today, this AVS and CMS system is functioning in a real-world environment handling the calibration quoting needs and workflows for hundreds of body shops across the country.”
ADAS Assist is available now to collision repair shops and calibration. For more information or to request an account, call (402) 315-5800 or visit ADASAssist.net.

Ranger Division of BendPak has introduced the next-generation DST Series wheel balancer, the DST30PX. As shops face larger OEM wheel assemblies and heavy aftermarket truck tires, older balancing platforms can slow production. The DST30PX is built to handle oversized wheels and prevent bottlenecks with a new hood design, larger shaft and overhauled structural chassis.

The hood accommodates a wider range of tire shapes and sizes, including oversized off-road and fleet tires, without repositioning. An open-side design allows wider tires, aggressive offsets and bulky sidewalls to slide in more easily, reducing setup time and enabling operators to position wheel assemblies up to 43 inches in diameter.

Ranger reinforced the chassis and hood assembly to handle the added mass of larger assemblies without flexing, compromising alignment or generating excess vibration. The added rigidity helps maintain consistent measurements for accuracy. A 40 mm shaft increases stiffness and accuracy for heavier wheels while supporting standard cones and accessories.

“The Ranger DST30PX represents a fundamental shift in how modern shops handle today’s radically heavier, oversized wheel configurations,” said Sean Price, director of product development for BendPak Inc. “By optimizing the physical layout and integrating a high-precision sensor array, we ensure technicians can mount, spin and perfectly balance oversized assemblies without a single second of wasted motion — turning massive wheel packages into a rapid, routine six-second floor-to-floor operation.”

The DST30PX features a 64-tooth magnetic transducer encoder with precision-cut square teeth to convert rotary position into a digital electronic signal, helping achieve accurate profile readings and top-dead-center positioning for precise weight placement. The extra encoder resolution supports cleaner correction, smaller weight changes and better placement accuracy for performance wheels, larger tiresand customers sensitive to vibration.
User-friendly Design for Fast Turnarounds

The DST30PX streamlines repetitive wheel service by reducing unnecessary motion. Simple wheel data entry, precise rolling weight readings, automatic braking, manual or automatic hood-start operation, and a rapid cycle time help technicians balance more wheels with fewer errors.

A quick-release hub nut, side-position brake, top-dead-center weight indicator, and tiered placement indicators accelerate setup and correction. Onboard storage includes a high-volume top tray, side cone pegs, and a side shelf designed to accommodate Ranger Quick-Peel adhesive tape weight rolls.
- 145-lb. capacity, 30-in. wheel diameter range, and 43-in. max tire diameter
- Low-RPM balancing operation and six-second cycle time
- Dynamic, Static and Performance Alloy settings
- 16-bit processor and multi-directional quartz piezoelectric sensors
- Ergonomic controls and full-tilt LED display control panel
- Automatic braking and self-calibration

The DST30PX is positioned as an upgrade for shops seeking higher precision, faster workflow and an advanced measuring system for modern wheels without moving to a larger machine. It is ETL-certified to meet applicable UL and CSA safety standards in the U.S. and Canada. It comes with a starter kit of adhesive and clip-on steel wheel weights. Ranger Select setup and training is available.

He’s referencing the negativity now spreading around the dangers of AI, from models breaking containment to AI insiders debating the percentage chance that AI may kill all of humanity by the end of the decade. The argument has become so mainstream that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was recently parodied in a skit on “Saturday Night Live,” where the fictional character summed up the discourse, saying, “We do not condone what we are doing.”

Feldman, however, thinks the promise and potential that go hand in hand with AI developments are getting overlooked. He thinks AI leaders should spend more time telling people that AI could lead to a world where your grandkids will “never meet anybody who dies of cancer,” for instance, even if they have concerns about AI risks.

Clearly, Feldman has a vested interest in AI being successful, as the company’s customers include big names working with the technology, like OpenAI, Block, Figma, pharmaceutical giant GSK, and Lovable.
However, he’s pragmatic about weighing the trade-offs between risk and reward.
“I think what we have to say is that this technology is powerful,” he added. “We have to be thoughtful about it. We have to regulate it reasonably,” he added.
The chipmaker CEO also suggested that some of the negativity around AI has to do with how the data center industry has approached the new buildouts created by AI demand.

“As an industry, we weren’t super good for the past few years at working with local communities, particularly in the U.S. We — the industry — didn’t do what others have done in the power industry in oil and gas. They didn’t work with the community. They didn’t engage the community as they should have, and that was a problem,” Feldman said.

He compared the NIMBY-ism — “not in my backyard!” — of what’s going on in the U.S. with other countries, naming Brazil, Canada, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Mexico, and Sweden as markets where they’re encouraging companies to build data centers.
Feldman also wasn’t concerned that efficiency improvements would create less demand for his chips, or those from other companies competing with Nvidia, as Cerebras is.

“We can do our job as hardware vendors to make our compute more efficient, and then the model makers can do improved work in making their models more efficient to achieve the same goals. All of this has to come together to make meaningful strides forward,” he noted.
